title: Memory: Sensory, Short-Term, Long-Term; Levels of Processing
summary: Whole report method; sensory memory; short-term memory (STM); long-term memory (LTM); levels of processing model (Craik & Lockhart); parallel distributed processing; spreading activation; hierarchical model of semantic memory.
objectives: Describe sensory, short-term, and long-term memory.
Describe parallel distributed processing and spreading activation.
Explain hierarchical model of semantic memory.
revision: Memory systems: sensory → STM (7±2 chunks) → LTM (unlimited). Levels of processing: structural → phonemic → semantic (deep = best retention). PDP = distributed networks. Semantic memory = hierarchical (cognitive economy).
confusions: Confusing STM capacity (7±2) with LTM capacity (unlimited).
Believing shallow processing leads to good retention.

notes.t: Sensory memory briefly holds sensory information (iconic for visual, echoic for auditory) before it decays or is transferred to short-term memory.
STM holds limited information (7±2 chunks) for about 15-30 seconds without rehearsal.
LTM has large capacity and can store information for extended periods, potentially a lifetime.
Craik & Lockhart proposed that memory depends on depth of processing: structural (shallow), phonemic (intermediate), semantic (deep). Deeper processing = better retention.
PDP models propose that memory is distributed across interconnected networks of simple processing units, not stored in single locations.
Activation spreads from one node to related nodes in semantic networks, explaining priming effects.
Collins & Quillian's model proposes concepts stored hierarchically with properties at the highest possible level (cognitive economy).
UGC NET frequently asks about levels of processing (deep = semantic = better retention) and the multi-store memory model.
